notes.b: When a chemist makes a substance, the amount collected is almost never the amount the equation predicts. Three linked terms describe the amount made, the amount that was possible, and how the two compare.
points: Yield is the amount of a product obtained from a reaction.

Theoretical yield is the maximum amount of product that could be formed from the given amounts of reactants. It is calculated from the balanced equation, assuming the reaction goes to completion and all of the limiting reactant (the reactant that runs out first) becomes the desired product.
Actual yield is the amount of product actually obtained, measured in practice, in the laboratory or in industry. It is what you weigh or measure at the end, not what the equation predicts.
Percentage yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100. It measures how efficiently reactants are converted into the desired product, so 100% would be perfect conversion.

The actual and theoretical yields must be in the same units: both grams, both moles, or both gas volumes at the same temperature and pressure. Gas volumes change with temperature and pressure, so a comparison is only fair under the same conditions.
notes.tip: Percentage yield is actual divided by theoretical, not the other way round. Never compare grams with moles: convert so both are in the same units. Exams ask you to define theoretical yield, actual yield and percentage yield.

notes.h: Method for theoretical and percentage yield (skills)
notes.b: Every yield question follows the same four steps. The theoretical yield comes from the equation and the amount of starting material; only the last step brings in what was actually collected.
points: Step 1: Write the balanced equation, because the coefficients (the numbers in front of each formula) give the mole ratio between reactant and product.
Step 2: Find the moles of the reactant that decides the amount of product, the one not in excess (excess means more than enough, so some is left over). Moles = mass ÷ molar mass.
Step 3: Use the mole ratio to find the moles of product, then convert to grams (or a gas volume). This is the theoretical yield.
Step 4: Percentage yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100.
notes.tip: The theoretical yield is worked out from the reactant that is not in excess. Working out which reactant that is, when the question doesn't say, is Higher Level (Limiting reagents).

notes.b: Ethene is made by dehydrating ethanol (removing the elements of water from it). This example follows the four steps for a reaction with a 1 : 1 ratio and shows the yield worked out from a mass and then from a gas volume.
points: Question: 4.60 g of ethanol was dehydrated to ethene and 1.96 g of ethene was collected. The equation is C₂H₅OH → C₂H₄ + H₂O, and the preparation is in “Investigation: preparing ethene”.
Moles of ethanol = 4.60 ÷ 46 = 0.100 mol (M of C₂H₅OH is 46 g mol⁻¹). The ratio is 1 : 1, so the theoretical yield is 0.100 mol of ethene.
Theoretical mass of ethene = 0.100 × 28 = 2.80 g (M of C₂H₄ is 28 g mol⁻¹).
A gas yield can also be compared by volume. One mole of gas occupies 22.4 L at STP (standard temperature and pressure), so 0.100 mol of ethene is 2.24 L at STP.
If 1.50 L of ethene (at STP) were collected, the percentage yield would be (1.50 ÷ 2.24) × 100 = 67.0%.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to calculate the percentage yield of an organic preparation, such as ethene, from given masses or volumes. Keep to one kind of unit: masses with masses, volumes with volumes.

notes.h: Worked example: preparing an ester (sample data)
notes.b: An ester is made by refluxing (boiling with a condenser so vapour returns to the flask) a carboxylic acid with an alcohol and an acid catalyst (a substance that speeds up the reaction without being used up). Here the ethanol is in excess, so the ethanoic acid decides the theoretical yield.
points: Question: 6.00 g of ethanoic acid was refluxed with excess ethanol and an acid catalyst, and 5.72 g of pure ethyl ethanoate was obtained. The equation is CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O.
Moles of ethanoic acid = 6.00 ÷ 60 = 0.100 mol (M of CH₃COOH is 60 g mol⁻¹), so the theoretical yield is 0.100 mol of ethyl ethanoate (the ratio is 1 : 1).
Theoretical mass = 0.100 × 88 = 8.80 g (M of CH₃COOC₂H₅ is 88 g mol⁻¹).

The yield is well below 100% mainly because esterification (making an ester) is reversible and reaches equilibrium, a balance in which reactants and products are both present. The preparation is in “Tests, reaction schemes and preparing an ester”.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to calculate the percentage yield of an organic preparation, and an ester is one of the examples. Base the theoretical yield on the reactant that is not in excess.

notes.b: Aspirin is made from salicylic acid in a 1 : 1 ratio, so this is another single-step yield calculation. Here the product was dried and purified before weighing.
points: Aspirin (C₉H₈O₄, M = 180) is made from salicylic acid (C₇H₆O₃, M = 138). One mole of salicylic acid gives one mole of aspirin.
Moles of salicylic acid = 2.76 ÷ 138 = 0.0200 mol, so the theoretical yield is 0.0200 mol of aspirin.
Theoretical mass of aspirin = 0.0200 × 180 = 3.60 g.
2.52 g of dry, recrystallised aspirin was obtained (recrystallised means purified by dissolving and letting crystals form again). The percentage yield = (2.52 ÷ 3.60) × 100 = 70.0%.

notes.h: Working back from a yield (sample data)
notes.b: Sometimes the percentage yield is given and you must find how much reactant to start with, or how much product will actually be collected. The calculation runs in the opposite direction, so the theoretical yield must be found first.
points: Question: what mass of ethanoic acid is needed to make 5.00 g of ethyl ethanoate if the yield is 65.0%?
Because only 65.0% of the possible product is obtained, the theoretical yield needed is larger: 5.00 ÷ 0.650 = 7.69 g of ethyl ethanoate.
Moles of ethyl ethanoate = 7.692 ÷ 88 = 0.08741 mol, which equals the moles of ethanoic acid needed, since the ratio is 1 : 1.
Mass of ethanoic acid = 0.08741 × 60 = 5.24 g (M of CH₃COOH is 60 g mol⁻¹).
To go from a percentage yield to an actual yield, use actual yield = theoretical yield × (percentage ÷ 100). For example, 15.0% of a theoretical 0.960 L of gas is 0.144 L, which is 144 cm³.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to calculate the actual mass or volume of product from a given percentage yield. Check that your answer is in the unit the question asks for, for example cm³ rather than L.

notes.h: Why the actual yield is less than the theoretical yield
notes.b: In practice the actual yield is almost always below the theoretical yield. There are several separate causes, some chemical and some to do with handling the product.
points: The reaction may not go to completion. Many organic reactions are slow or reversible and reach equilibrium, for example esterification, so some reactant is left unconverted.
Side reactions form other, unwanted products from the same reactants. For example, some ethanol forms other products instead of ethene, so less ethene is made.
Product is lost during transfer, filtration, separation and purification. For example, some product stays dissolved in the solvent after recrystallisation, or sticks to glassware and filter paper.
The reactants may be impure, so less of the real reactant is present than the mass suggests. A volatile product or reactant (one that evaporates easily) may also be lost as vapour.
A percentage yield above 100% means the product is impure or not fully dry, for example still containing water or solvent. The true yield can never exceed 100%.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to give reasons why the actual yield is less than the theoretical yield, so learn several with an example each. A yield over 100% is a sign of an impure or wet product, not a better reaction.

notes.b: Yield is not just a number in an exam question. It decides how much a process costs and how much waste it creates, and in multi-step syntheses (making a compound through a series of reactions) the losses add up.
points: In industry, a higher percentage yield means less raw material, energy and cost per kilogram of product, and less waste to treat or dispose of. This links yield to sustainability (making products while using fewer resources and creating less waste).

Pharmaceuticals (medicines) are made in many steps from simpler precursors (the starting compounds), so a low yield at each step makes the overall yield very small. There is more on this in “Organic products and pharmaceuticals”.

Overall yield of a multi-step synthesis = the product of the fractional yields of the steps, because each step only has what the one before delivered. For example, two steps of 80% and 75% give 0.80 × 0.75 = 0.60, an overall yield of 60%.

keyTerms.definition: The amount of a product obtained from a reaction.
The maximum amount of product that could form from the given amounts of reactants, calculated from the balanced equation.
The amount of product actually obtained in practice, in the laboratory or in industry.
The actual yield divided by the theoretical yield, multiplied by 100.
The actual yield divided by the theoretical yield, before multiplying by 100.
The product of the fractional yields of each step in a multi-step synthesis.
A reaction that forms unwanted products from the same reactants as the desired reaction.
A reaction that proceeds in both directions and reaches equilibrium, so it may not go to completion.

questions.prompt: Define theoretical yield and percentage yield, and give two reasons why the actual yield of a product is usually less than the theoretical yield.
questions.model: Theoretical yield is the maximum amount of product that could be formed from the given amounts of reactants, calculated from the balanced equation, assuming the reaction goes to completion. Percentage yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100. Two reasons: the reaction may be reversible and reach equilibrium, so some reactant is left unconverted; and product is lost during transfer, filtration and purification. A side reaction forming unwanted products is also a valid reason.

questions.prompt: 9.20 g of ethanol was dehydrated to ethene: C₂H₅OH → C₂H₄ + H₂O. 3.36 L of ethene, measured at STP, was collected. Calculate the theoretical volume of ethene at STP and the percentage yield.
questions.model: Moles of ethanol = 9.20 ÷ 46 = 0.200 mol. The ratio is 1 : 1, so moles of ethene = 0.200 mol. Theoretical volume of ethene = 0.200 × 22.4 = 4.48 L at STP. Percentage yield = (3.36 ÷ 4.48) × 100 = 75.0%.

questions.prompt: 3.00 g of ethanoic acid was heated under reflux with excess methanol and a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid; 2.59 g of methyl ethanoate (M = 74) was obtained: CH₃COOH + CH₃OH ⇌ CH₃COOCH₃ + H₂O. Calculate the percentage yield and suggest why it is less than 100%.
questions.model: Moles of ethanoic acid = 3.00 ÷ 60 = 0.0500 mol. The ratio is 1 : 1, so theoretical moles of methyl ethanoate = 0.0500 mol. Theoretical mass = 0.0500 × 74 = 3.70 g. Percentage yield = (2.59 ÷ 3.70) × 100 = 70.0%. The yield is less than 100% because the reaction is reversible and reaches equilibrium, so some reactant is left unconverted; and some product is lost during separation and purification.
